Long-travel vs. leveling on the Raptor platform — ExpeditionPortal

summary: Do not put a spacer or coil "lift kit" on a Raptor the way you would a Wrangler. The truck already has more suspension travel than most lifted rigs. What you actually want is enough front height to clear 37s without ruining the geometry — and for most owners that's a preload adjustment plus upper control arms, not a lift.
description:
The Raptor leaves the factory as a long-travel desert truck. Gen 1 (2010–2014) runs Fox 2.5 internal-bypass shocks with roughly 11–12 inches of travel; Gen 2 (2017–2020) steps up to Fox 3.0 bypass with Live Valve on later trucks; Gen 3 (2021+) replaces the rear leaf pack entirely with a five-link coil setup and pushes rear travel past 14 inches. Bolting a traditional suspension lift onto any of these works against the engineering — it raises the center of gravity, steepens CV and driveshaft angles, and on the IFS front end it pulls the suspension out of its designed operating window. The factory ride and high-speed composure are the whole point of the truck. Protect them.

So when a Raptor owner says "lift," what they almost always need is tire clearance. From the factory the Gen 1 and Gen 2 wear 35s; Gen 3 ships on 35s with a factory 37 package on the higher trims. Stepping up to 37s on a truck that didn't come with them is the most common reason to raise the front, and the honest answer is that you need surprisingly little height — typically 1.5 to 2 inches up front to keep the tire off the fender liner at full stuff and full lock.

The cheapest legitimate path is front coilover preload. The factory Fox front coilovers have a threaded preload collar; winding it up raises the front of the truck by compressing the spring slightly more. On most trucks you can pull 1 to 1.5 inches this way for the cost of an alignment afterward. The tradeoff is real and worth stating plainly: adding preload stiffens the initial ride and reduces available up-travel, so don't chase more than about an inch this way or you'll trade the Raptor's signature plushness for height you didn't need.

Past that, the right hardware is a leveling spacer kit (RPG, AccuTune, and SVC all sell front spacers in the $250–400 range) paired with aftermarket upper control arms. The factory UCAs run out of clearance and ball-joint articulation once you raise the front, so quality uniball arms — Camburg is the reference, around $850 — restore proper geometry, add caster back for on-center steering feel, and stop the ball joint from binding at the top of its range. For a truck that mostly sees highway and moderate trail on 37s, preload plus UCAs is the complete answer.

The full long-travel (LT) kit is a different category entirely. SVC Offroad, Foutz, Camburg, and RPG build kits that widen the front track by several inches, relocate or replace the lower arms, and add three or more inches of wheel travel. These are $6,000–15,000 installed, often require trimming or welding, and are aimed at owners running the truck hard in open desert. An LT kit is a genuine capability upgrade — and overkill for anyone whose hardest use is a fire road.

For a preload-and-UCA leveling job:

1. Support the truck on jack stands at the frame and let the front suspension hang. Confirm the coilovers are unloaded before touching the preload collar.
2. Measure current ride height at a fixed reference (center of hub to fender lip) on both sides and write it down.
3. Loosen the preload collar lock ring and wind the adjuster up evenly on both sides — count the threads so left and right match exactly. Uneven preload gives you a truck that sits crooked.
4. Install the upper control arms: remove the factory UCA (ball-joint nut at the knuckle, two pivot bolts at the frame), transfer or set the new uniball arm, and torque to the manufacturer's spec.
5. Re-load the suspension, roll the truck, and re-measure ride height. Confirm you hit your target and that both sides match within about 1/8 inch.
6. Get a full alignment. Raising the front changes caster and camber, and a Raptor that's out of caster wanders at speed — non-negotiable on a truck built to be driven fast.

For a full LT kit, follow the manufacturer's manual; these are multi-day fabrication-adjacent installs and outside the scope of a leveling write-up.

The biggest mistake is treating the Raptor like a body-on-frame solid-axle truck and stacking spacers to chase 3 or 4 inches. You'll get CV plunge, accelerated boot and joint wear, a harsh ride, and you'll have spent money making the truck worse. If you find yourself wanting that much height, what you actually want is a long-travel kit, not a lift.

Second: don't skip the UCAs once you go past about an inch of front height. Running the factory arms raised puts the ball joint near the end of its travel, which wears it out fast and can bind at full droop. The arms are the difference between "raised correctly" and "raised until something breaks."

Third, the alignment is not optional and not a place to save money. Caster is what keeps the truck planted at 70 mph on a dirt road, and it's the first thing you lose when you raise the nose.

A preload-only level is effectively free plus a $120–150 alignment. A spacer-plus-UCA leveling package lands around $1,100–1,400 in parts (RPG/AccuTune/SVC spacer ~$300, Camburg UCAs ~$850) plus alignment, and a weekend in the garage. A full long-travel kit is $6,500 (SVC +3.5") to $9,500+ (Foutz) in parts before professional installation, which most owners pay for.

Before you spend anything, confirm your generation — Gen 1, Gen 2, and Gen 3 front ends are different and parts are not interchangeable. If your only goal is fitting 37s, read the [Raptor tire fitment guide](/db/?v=raptor) first; you may find the clearance you need with preload alone. And if your real complaint is ride quality rather than height, the [shock service and upgrade path](/db/?v=raptor) is the better place to put the money.

title: Upper Control Arms on the Raptor — When the Factory Arms Become the Weak Link

citations.title: Camburg Raptor UCA product page
Raptor front end wear discussion — UCA and ball joints

alternatives.name: OEM replacement arms
alternatives.notes: Correct choice if the truck stays near stock height and sees moderate use — factory arms are well-engineered for the stock travel range.

summary: Aftermarket upper control arms earn their cost on a Raptor in two cases: you've added travel or larger tires beyond stock geometry, or you've worn out the factory ball joints from hard desert miles. For a stock-height truck on factory-size tires, OEM replacement arms are the honest answer.
description:
The Raptor's factory upper control arms are not a design flaw. Ford specced them for the truck's substantial stock travel, and they hold up well in normal use. The case for aftermarket arms is specific, and it's worth being clear-eyed about whether you're in it.

Two failure modes drive UCA upgrades on these trucks.

**Ball joint wear from desert miles.** Repeated full-travel cycling at speed — the exact thing the Raptor is built to do — works the factory ball joint harder than any other front-end component. Symptoms: a clunk over sharp bumps at the top of travel, visible play when you rock the wheel at 12 and 6 with the truck on stands, or uneven inner-edge tire wear that an alignment doesn't fix. Factory ball joints on hard-used trucks can be done by 50,000–70,000 miles.

**Geometry past stock range.** If you've added a coilover with more travel, a mid-travel kit, or you're running 37s with a leveling change, the factory arm's ball joint operates near the edge of its articulation range at full droop. That binds the joint, accelerates wear, and on aggressive setups can limit usable droop travel. Aftermarket arms with uniball or high-articulation joints fix the operating angle.

If neither describes your truck, replace worn factory arms with OEM and spend the difference on a shock rebuild — it'll do more for how the truck drives.

This is the real decision when buying aftermarket arms.

**Uniball arms** (Camburg, RPG, most race-oriented options) use a spherical bearing — maximum articulation and strength, zero compliance. The tradeoffs are honest ones: uniballs transmit more road noise, they're exposed to dust and water, and they need inspection and eventual replacement like any wear part. In Phoenix-style desert dust, expect to service uniballs every 30,000–50,000 miles. Dust boots help and are worth ordering.

**Sealed ball joint arms** (SPC and similar) trade a little articulation for weather sealing and quiet street manners. For an overland or daily-driven build that sees real trail miles, these are usually the better fit.

This is achievable in a home garage with the truck on stands, but front suspension work carries real consequences for getting it wrong — these torque values and this hardware locate the wheel that steers the truck.

1. Truck on stands at the frame, wheel off, support the lower control arm with the jack to keep the coilover compressed safely.
2. Disconnect the ABS line and brake line brackets from the factory arm.
3. Separate the upper ball joint — a proper separator tool, not a pickle fork if you're keeping any parts.
4. Unbolt the arm's pivot bolts from the frame. Note cam/alignment washer positions if present.
5. Install the new arm, torque pivot bolts **at ride height** — torquing rubber-bushed arms at full droop preloads the bushings and kills them early. Uniball-pivot arms don't care, but check the manufacturer's instructions.
6. Seat the ball joint stud, torque to the arm manufacturer's spec, new cotter pin or lock per design.
7. Reconnect lines, wheel on, torque lugs, and book an alignment before any real driving.

SPC adjustable arms run about $700/pair and add caster adjustability that helps 37-inch-tire trucks track straight. Camburg uniball arms run about $950. RPG billet arms are $1,200+ and are race-grade overkill for most builds — which is exactly the kind of thing Trail Manual will tell you before you spend the money. Add an alignment ($120–$180) to every option; it's not optional after control arm work.

title: Why Gen 2 Raptor Rear Leaf Springs Sag and What to Do About It

parts.name: Deaver spring re-arch (Gen 2 Raptor rear pack)
Ford Racing rear leaf spring pack replacement (Gen 2)
Roadmaster Active Suspension leaf spring add-on
Rancho RS66R leaf spring add-a-leaf kit (F-150 compatible)

citations.title: Deaver Springs Raptor leaf spring service
Gen 2 Raptor rear spring sag community documentation

summary: Gen 2 Raptor rear leaf springs sag under hard use — particularly trucks that see regular desert running, heavy loads, or frequent high-speed whoops. Re-arching is the budget fix. A full spring swap is the right fix. An add-a-leaf is a Band-Aid.
description:
The Gen 2 Raptor's rear suspension is a multi-leaf spring pack, not the coilover setup many performance trucks use. Ford chose leaf springs for load-carrying capacity and to keep towing ratings viable. The tradeoff is that leaf springs take a set under sustained heavy load or extreme impact — they sag, and the truck sits lower in the rear than it did from the factory.

The factory rear leaf pack was designed for a range of uses from highway cruising to moderate desert running. Sustained high-speed whoop running — the kind of use the Raptor was built to do — generates repeated high-impact compression loads on the spring pack. Over time, the spring steel takes a permanent set and doesn't return to its original arc. The truck sits lower at the rear, ride quality changes, and handling balance shifts.

This is not a defect. It's wear. But it's worth understanding because a used Raptor with a sagged rear sits noticeably lower than a fresh truck, handles differently, and may bottom out more easily.

**Signs of rear spring sag:**
- Rear of truck sits lower than factory spec — measure from the ground to the top of the rear wheel arch and compare to factory spec
- Rear bottoms out on impacts it previously handled
- Truck looks tail-low, especially compared to photos from new

A spring shop (Deaver, National Spring, or a local spring shop) removes the spring pack, heats the individual leaves, and re-bends them back to the factory arc. This restores original ride height and spring rate. It is a legitimate repair, not a hack.

**Realistic expectations:**
- Re-arched springs will sag again under the same use conditions — the spring steel has memory and was already fatigued once
- Re-arching is appropriate for trucks that see moderate use and where budget is the primary constraint
- Not appropriate for trucks that will continue to see hard desert use — the re-arched springs will sag faster than new springs

Replacing the spring pack with new Ford Racing springs (or a quality aftermarket equivalent) restores original spring rate and arc with new steel. This is the correct long-term fix for trucks that see real use.

Ford Racing offers replacement leaf pack assemblies specific to the Gen 2 Raptor. Installation is a straightforward bolt-in job — remove the U-bolts, drop the axle, swap the pack, reinstall. A good shop can do this in 3–5 hours.

Aftermarket options include Deaver's Gen 2 Raptor-specific spring packs. Deaver builds springs for off-road race trucks and their Raptor-specific packs are respected. They offer options from near-stock to increased spring rate for more consistent bottoming control under heavy use.

An add-a-leaf adds a supplemental leaf to the existing pack, increasing spring rate and ride height. This is the cheapest option and the least appropriate.

The problem: adding a leaf to a fatigued pack increases spring rate but doesn't restore the arc of the original leaves — the sag comes from the main leaves losing their arc, and an add-a-leaf doesn't change that. The truck rides firmer but may still sit low. Add-a-leaf is appropriate for trucks that need increased load capacity or are routinely towing near their limit. It's not a spring sag fix.

Several companies offer rear coilover conversion kits for the Gen 2 Raptor. These replace the leaf pack entirely with a coilover setup. This is a different truck after conversion — the ride quality changes significantly, load capacity drops, and the towing capability is reduced. This is a build decision, not a maintenance decision. It costs $3,500–$6,000 in parts before installation.

If your use case is pure desert performance and you're not towing, it's worth investigating. If you use the truck for towing or carrying loads, this path eliminates that capability.
steps: Measure current rear ride height — floor to wheel arch at the center of the rear wheel, truck empty, on flat ground
Compare to factory spec (varies slightly by trim — verify in Ford's documentation for your year)
If sag is 1" or less: re-arch is appropriate if budget is constrained; spring pack replacement for long-term fix
If sag is more than 1.5": full spring pack replacement is the correct call
Remove factory U-bolts and leaf spring mounting hardware (penetrating oil on hardware — these fasteners corrode)
Install new spring pack and new U-bolts — do not reuse old U-bolts on a spring pack replacement
Torque U-bolts and all leaf spring fasteners to factory spec (consult Ford service manual for your year)
Re-check torque after 100 miles
pros: Full spring pack replacement restores factory performance at reasonable cost
Deaver and Ford Racing aftermarket options offer improved durability over OEM
Re-arch is a legitimate budget option for moderate-use trucks
cons: Add-a-leaf does not fix spring sag — it changes spring rate only
Re-arched springs will sag again faster if use continues unchanged
Coilover conversion eliminates towing capacity and is a significant project
Leaf spring hardware (U-bolts, end bolts) corrodes — budget for replacement hardware regardless of which fix you choose

title: Shock Upgrade for the Gen 1 Raptor — Fox 3.0, King 2.5, and RCD Options

parts.name: Fox 3.0 Factory Series Front Coilovers (pair) — Raptor-specific valving
Fox 3.0 Factory Series Rear Shocks (pair) — Gen 1 Raptor

citations.title: Fox 3.0 vs King 2.5 Raptor comparison — RaptorForum community
Gen 1 Raptor suspension travel specs — Ford Media technical release
Bypass shock explained — Fox Factory technical resource

summary: The factory Fox shocks on the Gen 1 Raptor are a genuine performance baseline — but at 50,000+ miles or when you're running the truck hard in the desert, upgrading to a Fox 3.0 or King 2.5 is the single highest-impact suspension dollar you can spend.
description:
Ford's SVT team fitted the Gen 1 Raptor with internal bypass Fox shocks from the factory — a setup that was genuinely premium for a production truck in 2010. Internal bypass shocks use ports positioned along the shock body that progressively restrict damping as the shock approaches the end of its travel, providing soft compliance in the mid-stroke and firm control at full compression and rebound. It's the same technology used in Baja prerunner builds. The factory tune is competent, but it is a mass-production valving spec — one tune for every driving style, weight load, and terrain type. An aftermarket 3.0 or 2.5 diameter shock built specifically for the Raptor can be valved for your actual use: loaded overland touring, high-speed desert whoops, or mixed trail and pavement.

The Fox 3.0 Factory Series front coilovers are the most popular upgrade path. Going from the factory 2.0" diameter internal bypass to a 3.0" body doubles the oil volume, which translates directly to heat resistance — the leading cause of shock fade on a heavily used truck. For desert high-speed driving (the Raptor's core use case), more oil volume means the shocks stay consistent through longer runs. Fox's factory series shocks for the Raptor are pre-valved and ready to install; if you want custom valving, Fox's Racing Series with a custom tune is available at a higher price. King 2.5 OEM Performance is the competing choice: slightly smaller body than the Fox 3.0, but King's reputation for consistency and their excellent warranty make them the preference for some users. RCD's 3.0 coilovers come in at a higher price point but include extended travel provisions if you're also running a RCD lift kit.

The rear shocks are often overlooked relative to the front, but the Gen 1 Raptor's leaf-spring rear is where the factory tune falls short most noticeably on a loaded overland truck. Upgrading the rear Fox to a 3.0 or King 2.5 provides better high-speed dampening without harsh bottoming when the truck is loaded with camping gear.
steps: Set the front end at ride height on jack stands before removing anything — photograph your bumpstop gaps and coilover height for reference during reinstall.
Remove the front wheel and unplug any ABS sensor wire routed near the coilover.
Support the lower control arm with a jack. Remove the upper and lower coilover mounting bolts/nuts.

Remove the factory coilover assembly from the vehicle. If reusing the spring, compress it with a spring compressor and transfer it to the new shock body. If the new coilover ships with a spring, confirm the spring rate matches your intended use — most Raptor-specific kits include appropriate rates.

Install the new front coilovers and torque to spec (Ford spec: front lower 129 ft-lb, front upper 66 ft-lb — verify against your specific shock manufacturer's recommended torque as aftermarket mounting hardware may differ).
For rear shocks: support the axle with a jack, remove upper and lower shock bolts, and swap in the new unit. Torque rear lower to 76 ft-lb, rear upper to 66 ft-lb.
Set coilover collar height to match factory ride height before driving. Fine-tune after a 50-mile break-in.
Schedule a front alignment after any suspension work that changes coilover height.
pros: Larger shock body (3.0" vs factory 2.0") significantly reduces heat fade on hard desert runs
Custom or semi-custom valving options available for specific use cases
Fox and King both have strong warranty and rebuild programs — these shocks can be serviced rather than replaced
Improved consistency through long travel cycles; notable on back-to-back whoops runs
cons: Expensive — a full set of Fox 3.0 front and rear is $1,500+ before labor
Requires an alignment after front coilover replacement; budget $100–$150 for that
Does not increase suspension travel on its own — if you want more travel, you need a full lift kit
Factory Fox shocks at under 50,000 miles are genuinely good; this upgrade is most justified on high-mileage or heavily used trucks

title: FORScan on the Raptor: Read Codes, Enable Features, Avoid Trouble
tools_required: FORScan-compatible OBD2 adapter (OBDLink EX or MS-CAN/HS-CAN switchable)

parts.name: OBDLink EX USB adapter (recommended for FORScan)
FORScan license (free for personal use; extended license available)

citations.title: FORScan official documentation and supported adapters
Raptor FORScan feature-enable community spreadsheets

summary: FORScan is the tool that turns a generic OBD2 port into real access to a Raptor's Ford-specific modules — it reads manufacturer codes a $30 code reader can't see, datalogs Live Valve and EcoBoost parameters, and can enable factory features Ford left switched off (auto-lock, lighting tweaks, gauge options). It's free for personal use, but it needs the right adapter and a careful hand. Change one setting at a time and record the original value, because module programming can brick functions if you guess.
description:
A basic OBD2 scanner reads generic powertrain codes — enough to know the engine has a problem, rarely enough to know which one on a modern Ford. FORScan is software (Windows, Android, iOS) that talks to Ford's proprietary module network. With the right adapter it reads and clears manufacturer-specific codes from every module — engine, transmission, ABS, body, the Live Valve suspension controller — and lets you log live data the generic tools can't reach.

This is where people get stuck. Ford uses two CAN buses (HS-CAN and MS-CAN), and many cheap Bluetooth dongles only see one of them. To get full module access you need a FORScan-supported adapter that switches between buses. The community standard is the OBDLink EX (USB, rock-solid for Windows) at around $30, or a quality switchable ELM327 for mobile use. Buying a $10 generic dongle and expecting full FORScan function is the most common first mistake — it'll read the engine and nothing else.

- **Real diagnostics.** Pull and clear Ford-specific codes from any module. When the truck throws a vague warning, FORScan tells you which module and which code, not only "service engine."
- **Datalogging.** Log charge-air temps, fuel trims, fuel rail pressure, transmission temps, and Live Valve parameters under real driving conditions. This is how you catch heat soak, HPFP weakness, or transmission overheating with data instead of guesses.
- **Feature enabling.** Ford ships modules with features disabled that the hardware supports — things like auto-locking doors at speed, gauge display options, daytime running light behavior, and tailgate/lighting tweaks. FORScan can flip these "As-Built" configuration values.

Changing module configuration ("As-Built" data) is powerful and where you can cause real trouble. The rules that keep people out of the ditch:

- **Record the original value before you change anything.** Write down or screenshot the existing setting so you can put it back.
- **Change one setting at a time, then test.** Batch changes make it impossible to know what broke what.
- **Use vetted values.** The Raptor community maintains spreadsheets of known-good As-Built changes per model year. Use those rather than guessing hex values.
- **Keep battery voltage stable.** A dropping battery mid-write can corrupt a module. Have a charger/maintainer connected for any programming session.

Done carefully, feature enabling is reversible and safe. Done carelessly, it can disable functions or, in a worst case, require a dealer to reflash a module.

The big three mistakes: using a single-bus cheap adapter and wondering why half the modules are invisible; programming with a weak battery and corrupting a module; and changing multiple As-Built values at once so you can't isolate a problem. Respect all three and FORScan is one of the most useful tools a Raptor owner can have for under $30.

Adapter: $25–$60 depending on USB vs. switchable Bluetooth. FORScan software: free for personal use, with an inexpensive extended license for deeper programming. Total entry cost is roughly $30 — the cheapest serious diagnostic capability you can add to the truck, and it pays for itself the first time it saves a dealer diagnostic fee.
steps: Buy a FORScan-supported, bus-switchable adapter (OBDLink EX for Windows is the safe default)
Install FORScan and register the free personal license (an extended license unlocks more programming functions if you need them)
Connect with the ignition on, let FORScan identify the modules
For diagnostics: read codes across all modules, note the Ford-specific codes, clear only after you've recorded them
For datalogging: select the PIDs you care about (charge temp, fuel pressure, trans temp, Live Valve), log during a representative drive, review afterward
For feature enabling: connect a battery maintainer, open the As-Built section, record the current value, change one setting using a vetted community value, save, and test
If anything misbehaves, restore the original value you recorded
pros: Reads Ford-specific codes and datalogs parameters generic scanners can't touch
Free software; the only real cost is a $30 adapter
Enables factory features the hardware already supports
cons: Requires the correct bus-switchable adapter — cheap dongles see only part of the truck
Module programming can disable functions if done carelessly
The learning curve and hex-value configuration intimidate first-timers

title: Multimeter Electrical Diagnosis — Find the Fault Before You Throw Parts at It
skills_required: back-probing a connector without damaging the seal

parts.name: Test light (incandescent, not LED, for load testing)

citations.title: Ford F-150/Raptor workshop manual — wiring diagrams and pinpoint tests
Fluke — automotive voltage drop testing application notes

alternatives.name: Code reader / scan tool
alternatives.notes: An OBD2 scanner tells you which system is unhappy; a multimeter tells you why. They're complementary, not substitutes. Pull codes first with the approach in the scan-tool guide, then use the meter to confirm the actual fault before buying a part.

summary: A multimeter turns "the lights flicker sometimes" into a number you can act on. The single most useful automotive measurement isn't continuity or resistance — it's a voltage-drop test on a live circuit, which finds the bad grounds and corroded connectors that ohm tests miss. A $40 meter and twenty minutes beats replacing parts you didn't need.
description:
Electrical faults feel like black magic until you can measure them. They aren't — every fault is a break, a short, excess resistance, or a bad ground, and a meter distinguishes all four. The trick on a modern truck is testing without hacking into harnesses, which means back-probing connectors and reading voltage under load rather than with a dead circuit.

**Voltage (DC volts):** Probe between a circuit and ground with the circuit live. Battery should read 12.4–12.7V at rest, 13.5–14.7V running (the charging-system check from the [battery and charging](/db/?v=raptor) guide). A device that should see battery voltage but reads low has resistance upstream — a connector, a switch, or a ground.

**Continuity / resistance (ohms):** Power off, circuit disconnected. Near-zero ohms means an unbroken path; "OL" or infinite means a break. Use this to confirm a fuse is good, a wire isn't cut, or a ground strap is intact — but remember a wire can read continuous and still be too resistive under load. That's where voltage drop comes in.

**Voltage drop (the one most people skip):** Measure across a connection — both meter leads on the same circuit, one on each side of a joint — while current flows. A clean connection drops near zero. A corroded ground or connector drops a few tenths to a full volt, and that's your culprit. This is how you find a bad ground that an ohm test calls "fine," and it's the exact failure the [ground refresh](/db/?v=raptor) job is built to prevent.

Modern Ford connectors are sealed against exactly the dust and water a Raptor lives in. Piercing a wire to test it opens a path for corrosion that becomes next year's fault. Slide a back-probe pin alongside the wire from the rear of the connector, against the terminal, so the seal stays intact. For weatherpack and similar sealed connectors, back-probing from the wire side keeps the front seal closed.

When you must pierce — sometimes there's no back access — seal the hole afterward with a dab of liquid electrical tape or adhesive heat-shrink over the spot. An open puncture in a desert truck is a guaranteed return visit.

Say a bed light or compressor cuts out over washboard. Codes are clean. Start at the device: key on, back-probe its power and ground. If power reads full battery voltage and ground reads near zero volts to chassis, the device is the problem. If power sags when you wiggle the harness, you've localized it to that section — walk back toward the fuse box, testing voltage at each connector, until the voltage appears healthy on one side of a joint and sags on the other. That joint is the fault. Nine times out of ten on an older or hard-run truck, it's a ground or a corroded connector, not the accessory itself — which is why a meter saves the cost of the part you were about to throw at it.

A capable auto-ranging meter runs $25–$60 — the Klein MM400, AstroAI budget meters, and the Fluke 101 are all honest picks; you do not need a $300 Fluke for truck work. Add a $15 back-probe set and an $8 incandescent test light (incandescent, because it draws enough current to reveal high-resistance faults an LED tester hides). That's the whole kit. Pair it with the OBD2 [scan tool](/db/?v=raptor) and you can diagnose nearly any electrical complaint on the truck without a shop.

title: Raptor Diagnostics: OBD2 Scanners, TPMS Relearn, and What FORScan Can't Do

citations.title: FORScan Ford module programming reference
Ford TPMS sensor relearn procedure

summary: Two tools cover most of what a Raptor owner needs: a bidirectional OBD2 scanner to read and clear codes and run active tests, and a TPMS tool to relearn sensors after you swap between street and trail wheels. FORScan with a proper OBD adapter is the power-user option for Ford-specific module access, but it isn't a substitute for a TPMS activation tool, and it can't repair hardware. Buy the scanner that matches how deep you actually go.
description:
The Raptor throws the same diagnostic puzzles as any modern truck, plus a few specific to running multiple wheel sets and a turbo engine that owners like to monitor. Knowing which tool does what saves money and frustration. The deep Ford-module tool, FORScan, gets its own treatment in [FORScan for Raptor](/db/?v=raptor); this guide covers the broader toolkit and where each piece fits.

A scanner reads diagnostic trouble codes (DTCs), shows live sensor data, and — if it's bidirectional — commands active tests like cycling the ABS pump or the cooling fan. The tiers:

- **Budget Bluetooth ELM327 dongle ($20–$30)** paired with a phone app: reads and clears generic codes, shows basic live data. Fine for a check-engine light you want to understand before deciding what to do. Limited on Ford-specific codes.
- **Mid-range bidirectional scanner ($120–$250)** from Autel, Foxwell, or Topdon: reads manufacturer-specific codes, runs active tests, displays freeze-frame data. This is the practical sweet spot for a DIY Raptor owner.
- **FORScan with a quality adapter (OBDLink EX or MX+, ~$60 plus free software):** Ford-specific module access, the ability to read enhanced codes, and — for the experienced — program certain module settings. Powerful, but it's a software tool, not a hardware fix.

If you run a separate set of trail wheels (beadlocks, for instance) and street wheels, each set has its own TPMS sensors, and the truck needs to relearn the new sensor IDs when you swap. Without a relearn, you get a persistent TPMS warning and no real pressure data — exactly when you most want it, on the trail after airing down. A TPMS activation/relearn tool reads each sensor and writes the IDs to the truck. This is also covered from the pressure side in [Raptor Air-Down and TPMS](/db/?v=raptor); the tool is what makes a two-wheelset setup livable.

Some model years allow a relearn procedure through the dash menu or a drive-cycle; others require the tool. Know which your truck needs before you're standing at the trailhead with a blinking warning.

For most owners: one mid-range bidirectional scanner and, if you run multiple wheel sets, one TPMS tool. FORScan needs a compatible adapter — the cheap ELM327 dongles are unreliable for it, so budget for an OBDLink EX (USB) or MX+ (Bluetooth) if you want to run FORScan properly.

The biggest mistake is clearing codes to make a light go away without diagnosing the cause — on an EcoBoost, a cleared misfire or boost-related code hides a problem that's still there and may be doing damage under load. Read freeze-frame data and fix the root cause. The second is trying to run FORScan on a bargain ELM327 dongle; they drop connection mid-operation, and a dropped connection during module programming can leave a module in a bad state. The third is assuming any scanner does TPMS relearn — most don't; that's a separate tool.

A budget Bluetooth dongle is $20–$30. A capable mid-range bidirectional scanner runs $120–$250. A proper FORScan adapter is $40–$70 (the software is free). A TPMS relearn tool is $60–$120. For a Raptor owner who runs two wheel sets and likes to monitor the truck, a mid-range scanner plus a TPMS tool — roughly $250 total — covers nearly everything short of dealer-level programming.
steps: Match the tool to your needs — don't buy a $250 scanner for an occasional code read, and don't expect a $25 dongle to do Ford module work
To read a code: plug into the OBD2 port under the dash, key on, and pull the DTC plus freeze-frame data before clearing anything
Diagnose from the code and live data — clearing a code without fixing the cause only resets the countdown to the light returning
For TPMS relearn after a wheel swap: activate each sensor with the tool in the relearn sequence, then confirm all four (or five) report pressure
For FORScan: use only a known-compatible adapter, and read the documentation before changing any module setting — wrong values can disable features
pros: A bidirectional scanner pays for itself the first time it saves a diagnostic shop visit
A TPMS tool makes running separate trail and street wheels practical
FORScan unlocks Ford-specific data and settings for free, beyond generic scanners
cons: FORScan needs a quality adapter and the knowledge to use it safely — it can misconfigure modules
No single tool does everything; scanning and TPMS relearn are usually separate purchases
Clearing codes is not fixing problems, and it's a common trap to fall into

title: Converting to Beadlock-Capable Wheels on the Gen 2 and Gen 3 Raptor
tools_required: bead seating tool or air compressor

citations.title: Method Race Wheels Raptor fitment guide
Ford F-150 Raptor Gen 3 37 Package beadlock wheel specs

summary: The Gen 2 and Gen 3 Raptor factory forged 17x8.5 wheels are "beadlock-capable" — meaning the wheel accepts a bolt-on beadlock ring. The ring is sold separately. For extreme airing-down (under 10 PSI), beadlocks provide meaningful protection. Most Raptor owners don't need them.
description:
"Beadlock-capable" is a specific term. The factory Raptor forged wheels have a machined outer lip that accepts an inner and outer ring system — you can convert a factory wheel into a true beadlock by purchasing and installing the beadlock ring kit. This is not the same as installing a fully separate aftermarket beadlock wheel, though aftermarket options exist too.

A tire bead is the inner edge of the tire that seals against the wheel rim. Under normal inflation (30–45 PSI), the bead is held against the rim by air pressure. If you air down below approximately 8–10 PSI, that clamping force decreases enough that aggressive cornering or lateral force can break the bead — the tire rolls off the rim.

A beadlock clamps the outer tire bead mechanically between the wheel's outer lip and the bolt-on beadlock ring. This mechanical clamping is independent of air pressure. You can run 4–5 PSI in sand or rocky terrain without risk of the tire debeading.

**Justified cases:**
- Regular sand running at 5–8 PSI (Arizona dunes, coastal sand, Glamis)
- Technical rock crawling where tire deformation at low pressure is intentional
- Competition use

**Cases where beadlocks are overkill:**
- Desert whoops and high-speed running (Raptor home territory) — you're running 20–25 PSI for speed, not 5 PSI
- Trail use that doesn't go below 15 PSI
- Daily driving

Most Raptor owners who want beadlocks are buying them for aesthetics or for occasional hard use. That's a valid choice. But the honest answer is that the truck runs most of its intended mission at 18–25 PSI, which doesn't require beadlock clamping.

Gen 2 and Gen 3 base Raptors come with factory forged aluminum 17x8.5 wheels. These wheels are machined on the outer lip to accept a beadlock ring from Ford Performance. The ring bolts to the wheel using a series of ring bolts at specific torque values.

The conversion requires:
1. Dismount the existing tire from the wheel
2. Install the beadlock ring inner piece against the wheel
3. Mount the tire onto the wheel
4. Install the outer beadlock ring, threading the ring bolts through the ring into the wheel
5. Torque the ring bolts to spec in a star pattern — typically 21–25 ft-lb depending on the ring hardware
6. Inflate to seat the inner bead, then final-inflate to operating pressure

**Critical:** Beadlock ring bolts require periodic re-torquing. After the first 100 miles, retorque. Then every 3,000–5,000 miles or before any extended trail trip. A loose beadlock ring can cause vibration and, in severe cases, tire failure.

**Method Race Wheels 105 Beadlock** — well-established in the Raptor community. 17x8.5 in the correct bolt pattern (6x135mm). Forged, strong, proven. $300–$380 per wheel.

**SOTA Offroad Novakane Beadlock** — more budget-friendly option at $240–$280 per wheel. Heavier than Method but functional. Good choice if you want full beadlock without the full Method price.

When switching to aftermarket wheels, verify the hub bore (Ford F-150 is 87.1mm center bore) and confirm the offset. The factory Raptor wheel runs a high positive offset — going to a significantly different offset changes handling behavior and may affect brake caliper clearance.

Factory TPMS sensors are mounted in the valve stem area and can typically be transferred to aftermarket beadlock wheels. Verify the TPMS sensor mounting style (band-mount vs. valve-stem mount) matches your new wheel's mounting provision. A tire shop can handle the sensor transfer during the tire mounting process.
steps: Confirm your wheel's bolt pattern (6x135mm, 87.1mm center bore on all Gen 2/3 Raptors)
Choose factory ring kit (for factory wheels) or aftermarket beadlock wheels
Have tires professionally dismounted and remounted with beadlock ring installation
Torque beadlock ring bolts to specification in a star pattern
Check for vibration in the first 50 miles — ring bolts settling is normal, retorque if vibration develops
Retorque ring bolts at 100 miles, then every 3,000–5,000 miles
Transfer TPMS sensors to new wheels before mounting
pros: True tire security at low pressures in sand and rock terrain
Factory forged wheels are convertible without buying new wheels
Method and SOTA offer strong aftermarket options at reasonable prices
cons: Most Raptor use doesn't require beadlocks — honest assessment
Ring bolts require periodic retorquing — it's a maintenance item you cannot neglect
Aftermarket wheel offset changes can affect handling — verify before buying
Added weight per wheel (ring hardware adds 2–3 lbs)

title: Airing Down a Raptor — Pressures That Work, TPMS Behavior, and Reinflation That Doesn't Ruin the Day

citations.title: Ford Raptor owner's manual — TPMS operation
Tire pressure for sand and desert running

summary: For most Raptor desert running: 20–24 psi. Sand and dunes: 14–18 psi. Below 12 psi on non-beadlock wheels you're gambling with a debeaded tire. The TPMS light will come on at these pressures — it's expected, it's harmless, and it resets itself when you air back up.
description:
Airing down is the single highest-value, lowest-cost change you can make to how a Raptor rides off-pavement. The factory suspension gets the headlines, but the tires are the first spring in the system, and at street pressure they're a spring set to "concrete." Dropping 12–15 psi transforms small-bump compliance, traction, and how much abuse reaches the cab.

The Raptor is heavy — 5,700–6,000 lbs depending on generation — and runs a tall 35- or 37-inch tire with a strong sidewall. That combination means it tolerates lower pressures well but also punishes a debeaded tire with a long, heavy recovery.

- **Graded dirt and washboard:** 24–28 psi. Enough to calm the chatter without meaningful sidewall risk at speed.
- **General desert running, whoops, mixed terrain:** 20–24 psi. The sweet spot for most days. The truck rides dramatically better and the bead stays planted through hard cornering.
- **Soft sand and dunes:** 14–18 psi. Flotation is everything in sand; this is where the contact patch grows enough to keep the truck on top.
- **Below 12 psi:** beadlock territory. On standard wheels, hard side-loading at these pressures can roll the bead off the rim. Gen 3 trucks with the factory beadlock-capable wheels need the actual beadlock ring kit installed before the "capable" part is real.

Speed matters as much as terrain. Aired-down tires flex more and build more heat; at 18 psi, keep sustained speeds moderate and check sidewall temperature by hand when you stop. A sidewall too hot to rest your palm on wants more pressure or less speed.

Drop below roughly 25% under the door-jamb placard pressure and the low-pressure warning lights. Nothing else happens — no limp mode, no intervention. The light clears itself a few minutes after you reinflate above threshold. Gen 3 trucks with the 360 display will nag more visibly, but the behavior is the same.

Don't disable TPMS to silence the light. The system still catches the failure mode that matters: one tire losing pressure while the other three hold, which off-road usually means a puncture you haven't noticed yet. Glance at the per-tire readout when the light's on — four matched low numbers is your doing; one outlier is a problem.

A valve-core tool and patience works, but four 37s take a while. Two tools solve it:

- **ARB E-Z Deflator ($45):** removes the valve core, dumps air fast, gauge built in. One tire at a time, about 45 seconds per tire to drop 15 psi from a 37.
- **Staun automatic deflators ($90/set):** preset screw-on caps; thread one onto each tire and they all stop at your set pressure while you do something else. Set-and-forget, but recalibrating the preset is fiddly.

Airing down without a reinflation plan is how people end up driving 40 highway miles at 16 psi, which overheats sidewalls and is genuinely dangerous at speed. The math on compressors: a 37-inch tire from 16 to 38 psi is a lot of air, four times over.

A small cigarette-lighter compressor will technically do it in 25–30 minutes of duty-cycle-limited misery. A VIAIR 400P-class portable does all four in 10–12 minutes. An ARB twin on-board setup does it in about 6 and is always with the truck. For a truck this size used the way Raptors get used, the VIAIR 400P is the minimum that won't make you regret airing down, and it's the line item people skip and then buy anyway after the first trip.

Deflator $45–$90, gauge $15, compressor $310–$550. Call it $400 for a complete setup that turns every dirt mile the truck ever drives noticeably better. Nothing else in this price range touches that return.

title: The Spare Tire and Jack Problem on 35s and 37s — What Fits Under the Bed, and Why the Factory Jack Is No Longer Enough

parts.name: Safe Jack 6-ton bottle jack recovery kit
Pro Eagle 2-ton Big Wheel off-road jack

citations.title: Raptor 37 Performance Package spare details
Spare fitment under Gen 2 beds — measurements from owners

alternatives.name: Run a matching spare in the bed
alternatives.notes: Costs bed space and ~120 lb, gains a full-speed, no-compromise spare. The standard answer for desert trips; the under-bed compromise spare handles daily duty.

summary: A 35 fits in the factory under-bed spare location. A 37 does not — except on Gen 3 trucks with the factory 37 Performance Package, which got a revised carrier and a (slightly smaller-diameter spec) spare to make it work. If you've upsized aftermarket, your real options are: keep a 35 under the bed as a get-home spare, or carry a matching tire in the bed. And whichever you choose, the factory screw jack needs to be retired — it doesn't have the lift height to get a flat 37 off the ground on a drooped axle.
description:
The spare tire question gets ignored until the day it matters, usually somewhere with no cell signal. Work it out in the driveway with a tape measure, not on the trail.

The factory spare well between the frame rails behind the axle has hard limits set by the spare winch travel and the frame crossmember:

- **Stock-size spare (35x12.50 equivalent):** fits by definition — it is the factory arrangement.
- **Aftermarket 35 on a standard-width wheel:** fits on all generations. This is the painless answer.
- **37x12.50:** does not fit Gen 1/Gen 2 under-bed, period — diameter fouls before the winch seats it. Gen 3 non-37-package trucks are equally out of luck.
- **Gen 3 with the factory 37 package:** Ford solved it at the factory with carrier changes; if you have this truck, your spare situation is handled and your real question is the jack, below.

A mismatched spare is workable within reason: a 35 spare on a truck running 37s is roughly an inch of radius difference. Fine to drive home moderately on a free rear ratio; on the front of a 4WD-engaged truck or with the rear locker active, it grinds driveline components against each other — put the mismatched spare on the rear, drive in 2WD, and keep speeds sane. The locker/Torsen guide explains why mismatched diameters and torque-biasing differentials don't mix.

Lift the truck, add tire diameter, droop the suspension when the wheel comes off the ground — the factory bottle-screw jack runs out of stroke before a 37 clears. Test it once at home and you'll never trust it again. Real options:

1. **Safe Jack-style bottle jack kit (~$200–$300):** a 6-ton bottle jack with screw extensions and a base plate for sand. Compact, stores behind the seat, lifts from the axle so suspension droop doesn't eat the stroke. The pragmatic choice for most trucks.
2. **Pro Eagle off-road floor jack (~$350–$450):** wheels that roll on dirt, huge lift range, fast. The desert-crew standard, but it lives in the bed and costs bed space — pairs naturally with a bed-mounted spare.
3. **Exhaust-air or hi-lift jacks:** the hi-lift is the wrong tool on this truck — there's no bumper or slider lift point on a stock Raptor that's hi-lift-safe, and a 6,000 lb truck on a hi-lift in sand is a guillotine. Skip it unless your armor was specifically built for it.

Whatever jack you carry, add a 12"x12" base plate (or a chunk of 3/4" plywood) — every jack is only as good as the sand under it. And confirm your lug wrench actually fits the aftermarket lug nuts on your aftermarket wheels; spline-drive lugs with a missing key have stranded more trucks than flat tires have.

For real desert trips on 37s, the answer is a matching spare in the bed: bed-mounted carrier ($300–$700, bolts through the bed floor or to a rack), or strapped to a bed rack alongside the traction boards the sand recovery guide already has you carrying. Mind the weight — a 37 on a bead-lock-style wheel approaches 130 lb, mounted high and behind the axle, which the rear suspension feels. It's the right tradeoff for remote trips and the wrong one for commuting; many owners load the bed spare only for trips and run the under-bed 35 day to day.

Get-home setup: aftermarket 35 take-off on a cheap steel or factory take-off wheel under the bed ($150–$300 used) plus a Safe Jack kit ($250). Full desert setup: matching 37 spare mounted ($600–$900), carrier ($300–$700), Pro Eagle ($400). Check the spare winch mechanism while you're deciding — they seize from dust and disuse, and a spare you can't lower is decoration. Run it down and back up once a season with the dust management habits this truck already demands.

title: What Tires Actually Fit on a Raptor Without a Lift

citations.title: Ford F-150 Raptor Gen 2 factory spec — 315/70R17 BFG KO2
Gen 3 Raptor 37 Package specs

summary: Factory Gen 2 and Gen 3 base Raptors run 315/70R17 (equivalent to 35x12.5) BFGoodrich KO2s on 17x8.5 wheels. 37s on a Gen 3 require the factory 37 Package or a leveling kit plus minor clearance work.
description:
The Raptor was designed around large tires from day one. Gen 1 SVT ran 315/70R17 BFG All-Terrain T/A KO. Gen 2 moved to the KO2 in the same size. Gen 3 base continues with 315/70R17, and the optional 37 Package steps up to 37x12.5R17.

The SVT Raptor came from the factory on 315/70R17 BFG All-Terrain T/A KO (later KO2) tires on 17x8.5-inch forged aluminum wheels. This is equivalent to approximately 34.4" tall — commonly rounded to 35" in conversation.

Tire swaps on Gen 1: any 315/70R17 fits without modification. Moving to a true 35x12.5R17 adds a small amount of height (roughly 34.4" vs 35.0") — clearance is fine at full stuff with stock suspension in good condition. Rubbing at full lock-to-lock articulation is possible depending on the specific tire brand's width. Test before finalizing.

Same baseline as Gen 1 in concept, upgraded tire. The 315/70R17 KO2 is the OEM tire and the correct size for stock suspension. In practice, the Gen 2's suspension geometry was designed around this tire — it clears at full compression and full articulation.

Running true 35x12.5 (slightly taller and wider depending on brand): most 35x12.5R17 tires fit without modification, but the extra section width can cause contact at full compression depending on the tire brand's actual measured width. BFG's 315/70R17 is actually 12.4" wide; a 35x12.5 from another brand may be slightly wider and may require minor fender liner trimming.

**Running 37s on a Gen 2:** A leveling kit (typically 1.5"–2") creates enough clearance for 37x12.5R17 tires at full stuff. However, the factory 3.73 gear ratio becomes noticeably strained with 37s. Performance degrades meaningfully — acceleration, throttle response, and highway cruise RPM all shift unfavorably. If running 37s on a Gen 2, regearing to 4.10 or 4.56 is the right call.

The Gen 3 diverged into two tire specifications:

**Base Gen 3:** 315/70R17 BFG KO2 — same as Gen 2, no changes in fitment behavior.

**37 Package (optional):** 37x12.5R17 BFG KO2 on 17x8.5 forged beadlock-capable wheels, paired with 4.10 axle gears and upgraded Brembo brakes. This is a factory-engineered package — Ford sized the fenders, calibrated the ABS, and chose the gears specifically for 37s. It is not an afterthought.

Running 37s on a non-37-Package Gen 3: technically possible with a leveling kit, but you're missing the 4.10 gears that make the truck functional with the taller tires. The non-37-Package Gen 3 has 3.73 gears — the same penalty as Gen 2 with 37s.

At full suspension compression (both wheels droop), the Raptor's long-travel suspension moves the tire significantly upward relative to the body. Factory 315/70R17 clears in all four corners without issue. The concern zone is the front at full compression combined with full steering lock. On stock suspension with stock 315/70R17, clearance is designed in. Adding width (wider tire brand) or height (37s without a leveling kit) changes this.

A practical test: with the truck on flat ground, turn the wheel to full lock in both directions and bounce the front of the truck manually. If it rubs, you need more clearance before going off-road where actual full-compression events will happen.
steps: Confirm your generation and whether Gen 3 has the 37 Package (window sticker or door jamb)
For same-size replacements (315/70R17): any quality AT or MT tire in that size bolts on without modification
For 35x12.5 on Gen 1 or Gen 2: check the specific brand's measured section width before ordering — test for rub at full lock before trail use
For 37s on Gen 2 or non-37-Package Gen 3: plan for regearing to 4.10 or 4.56 and minor fender liner trimming
Torque lug nuts to factory spec (150 ft-lb on Gen 2, 150 ft-lb on Gen 3)
Reset TPMS after any wheel/tire change
pros: 315/70R17 is widely available from multiple quality manufacturers
37s on a factory 37-Package Gen 3 are properly integrated — no compromises
The 17-inch wheel size keeps tire costs lower than 20-inch equivalents
cons: 37s without the 4.10 gear package are a real performance compromise
Gen 2 with 37s needs regearing — that's $2,500–$4,000 in additional work
Some 35x12.5 tires are genuinely wider than the factory 315/70 — verify before buying

title: Tire Rotation and Road-Force Balance — Making 35s and 37s Wear Evenly and Run Smooth
tools_required: floor jack rated for the truck
skills_required: safely lifting and supporting the truck

parts.name: Anti-seize (for lug studs — use sparingly, see note)

citations.title: Ford F-150/Raptor owner's manual — wheel torque spec and rotation interval
Tire Industry Association — rotation patterns and road-force balancing

alternatives.name: Tire-shop rotation and balance
alternatives.notes: Most tire chains rotate free with a tire purchase and charge $15–$25 per tire for road-force balance. Worth paying for the road-force machine specifically — a standard spin balancer can't diagnose a tire that's round but pulls. Do your own rotations between their balances to stretch the interval.

summary: Big off-road tires on a heavy, powerful truck wear fast and unevenly if you ignore them — and a 35 or 37 that's even slightly out of balance shakes a Raptor hard enough to feel like a suspension problem. Rotate every 5,000–7,500 miles, balance on a road-force machine (not a basic spin balancer) whenever you mount new rubber or feel a vibration, and you'll get thousands of extra miles out of a $1,800 set of tires.
description:
Tire care is the cheapest performance and safety upgrade on the truck, and the most ignored. The same aggressive tread that earns its keep in sand and rock ([tire fitment](/db/?v=raptor) covers choosing it) is also soft, heavy, and quick to cup if it never moves position. A disciplined rotation and balance habit is the difference between replacing tires at 25,000 miles and at 45,000.

Rotate every 5,000–7,500 miles. For non-directional tires on the same-size wheels front and rear, the forward-cross pattern works: rears move straight forward, fronts cross to the opposite rear. Directional tires (check the sidewall arrow) only move front-to-back on the same side. If you run a staggered or different-size setup, rotation options narrow — front-to-back only on matching sizes.

Every rotation is a free inspection. Read the wear: feathering across the tread points to alignment (the [steering and alignment](/db/?v=raptor) guide covers toe and camber); cupping or scalloping points to balance or a tired shock; wear on both edges means chronic underinflation; a worn center strip means overinflation. Catch these patterns early and you fix a $90 alignment instead of buying tires.

Lug torque is not a place to guess. The Raptor's spec is in the 150 ft-lb range (verify the exact figure for your wheels — aftermarket wheels sometimes call for a different value). Tighten in a star/cross pattern in two passes, snug then final, with a torque wrench — never an impact gun for the final pass. Over-torquing warps rotors and stretches studs; under-torquing lets a wheel work loose. Re-check torque after the first 50–100 miles on any wheel you install, because the clamping load settles.

A light touch of anti-seize on the stud threads is fine in a dust-and-salt environment, but use it sparingly and know that lubricated threads reach the same clamping force at slightly lower torque — when in doubt, torque clean and dry to spec.

A standard spin balancer corrects weight imbalance — it makes the tire/wheel spin without wobble. It cannot detect a tire that's perfectly balanced but not perfectly round, and large off-road tires are frequently not perfectly round. A road-force balancer presses a loaded roller against the spinning tire and measures the force variation, then tells the tech how to match-mount the tire's stiff spot to the wheel's low spot to cancel it out.

This matters on a Raptor because a few pounds of road-force variation on a 35 or 37 produces a vibration that feels exactly like a driveline or [steering](/db/?v=raptor) problem — and people chase the wrong fix for months. If you have a smooth-tire vibration that survives a normal balance, ask specifically for road-force balancing and match-mounting before you touch anything in the suspension or driveline.

Rotation at home is free beyond your time and a torque wrench you should already own ($40–$70 for a decent 1/2-inch unit good to 150 ft-lb). Road-force balancing runs $15–$25 per tire and is worth every cent on big rubber. A tread-depth gauge is $8 and turns "looks fine" into a number. The whole habit costs almost nothing and is the single biggest lever on how long your tires last — pair it with correct [air-down and TPMS](/db/?v=raptor) discipline for the full picture.
